assign.request: Finish the manifest reset-recovery left incomplete: mine today's transcripts for every tracked file the 23:16 reset destroyed (only ~39 of an unknown total were listed), grade each recoverable yes/partial/no, state the total and the gone-for-good count plainly, do not restore anything.
assign.now: scoping a mechanical method instead of reading transcripts by hand
steps: Read reset-recovery's brief, lost.jsonl and task.jsonl
Find a mechanical way to enumerate every file the reset touched, not just what a git-status snapshot happened to catch
Cross-check that method against the mastermind's own independent count
Find the staged-but-never-committed files a plain git-status/mtime scan cannot see
Build a one-time index of every Read/Write/Edit call in the transcript archive
Classify all target files yes/partial/no against that index, using only evidence dated between the last commit and the revert
Write the complete lost.jsonl and the corrected page.js top line

log.msg: USAGE SNAPSHOT SKIPPED on purpose: this task's fence is reset-scope/** plus two named files in reset-recovery/ -- not ai/usage.json or ai/usage.jsonl -- so per new-task's own caveat (two agents already lost five days of samples this way on 2026-09-19) I did not touch either file.

METHOD DECISION, the key one: instead of hand-mining ~60 scoped git-status snapshots one at a time (what the brief suggested and what reset-recovery ran out of budget doing), I found a mechanical, complete way to answer 'which tracked files did the reset touch' -- their FILESYSTEM MTIME. A git reset --hard only rewrites a file's bytes (and therefore its mtime) when that file's working-tree content actually differs from the target commit; a file that was already clean is left alone. So every tracked file whose current mtime exactly equals the reset's own timestamp is, by construction, a file that had a real uncommitted edit at that instant. No transcript archaeology needed for this half of the list at all.

Confirmed the mechanism first: `git reflog show HEAD` shows exactly two 'reset: moving to HEAD' entries, at 2026-09-18 00:47:26-05:00 and 2026-09-19 23:16:41-05:00, both landing on 8b4ced8e -- matching the brief's 'it also happened on 2026-09-18' exactly. Converted 2026-09-19 23:16:41-05:00 to epoch: it spans two integer seconds (1789877800 and 1789877801, since the reset took a bit over one second to write everything). Checked a known-reverted file's mtime (.gitignore, Server/plugins/AILogs.js, public/app.js, Page.class.js) and all read exactly 1789877800 -- confirms the method against ground truth.

Ran `git ls-files -z | xargs stat` over all 6504 tracked files and kept every one whose mtime is 1789877800 or 1789877801: exactly 1043 files. This matches the mastermind's own independent count in mastermind-sonnet-run/task.jsonl (23:38:55 log line: '1043 files carry a 23:16 mtime') to the file -- strong cross-validation that this list is both correct and complete for the tracked-and-modified half of the loss. Added the 5 files reset-recovery already restored (their mtimes moved when rewritten, so the scan alone would miss them): framework.css, devbar.css, DevBar.js, tools.js, readme.md.

CHECKED for the 2026-09-18 00:47:26 reset's own separate damage: no tracked file's mtime matches that timestamp at all today. Reasoning: any file reverted then and never touched again would still carry that mtime now, and none do -- so every file that reset actually damaged was either (a) re-edited afterward and then caught again by the 23:16 reset (already in the 1043 above), or (b) already clean at 00:47 (nothing lost). I could not fully rule out every edge case here, so I am NOT claiming zero residual 9-18-only loss -- only that I found no filesystem evidence of any, and it is the best check available without a time machine.

SECOND LOSS CATEGORY the mtime method structurally cannot see: a file that was `git add`-staged today but never committed. A hard reset deletes those outright (they don't exist in the target commit's tree), so they vanish from disk AND from `git ls-files` -- there is no mtime to find because there is no file. This is exactly what happened to .claude/skills/minion/improvements.md and ai/2026-09-18/day.jsonl in reset-recovery's own list. To find the rest of this category I wrote a script scanning all 540 transcript files (1.2GB) for anything shaped like a git-status porcelain line (a two-letter code plus a path), restricted to hits timestamped between the last commit (2026-09-17 16:22:13) and the revert, then kept only the 'A'/'AM'-coded (staged) paths that are ALSO, right now, missing from both disk and `git ls-files`. Found 422 more files this way -- almost all of it two features: a 'public/layouts/browse' encyclopedia (263 files, mostly its own screenshots) and a 'public/framework/styles/system' design-study module (145 files), both staged the evening of 2026-09-18/19 and never committed.

TOTAL: 1043 (tracked, mtime-confirmed) + 5 (already restored, same cause) + 422 (staged-and-deleted) = 1470 distinct files lost real uncommitted work to the reset. I consider this a strong, largely mechanical count for the tracked-file half (1048) and a good-faith, cross-checked-but-not-provably-exhaustive count for the staged-file half (422) -- it depends on some agent's git status today having listed each staged path at least once, which is likely but not certain for every one of them. Lower bound 1470; the true number could be a little higher only in the staged-file category.

SEPARATE, NOT COUNTED IN THE 1470: public/framework/dev/DevBar/chat.js (reset-recovery's own top follow-up). It was never tracked or even staged, so the reset's own mechanism (which only touches the index/working-tree entries that exist in git) cannot have deleted it -- untracked files were supposed to survive intact, and this one didn't, for an unrelated and still-unknown reason. Left in lost.jsonl with reset-recovery's own investigation verbatim (it already found the file's one full Write in a transcript, so it is recoverable -- just not by anything this task's method would have found, since it never touches git at all).

RECOVERABILITY: built a one-time index of every Read result, Write and Edit call across all 540 transcripts (21,399 tool calls total, 3.3s to build) keyed by file path, then classified each of the 1470 targets: 'yes' if the LATEST touch on record before the revert (and after the last commit -- an earlier touch could already be baked into that commit, so it proves nothing about the lost diff) is a full Read or Write, or an Edit chain that has one of those as its anchor; 'partial' if only bare Edit diffs exist with no full base; 'no' if nothing in-window was found. IMPORTANT CORRECTION caught and fixed during this task: my first pass did not bound evidence to after the last commit, and it wrongly marked core/Page/Frame.js 'yes' off a stale Edit from 2026-09-06 -- 11 days before the commit it supposedly survived, i.e. certainly already IN that commit and irrelevant to what's actually lost. Re-ran with the commit-time floor; the honest numbers below are from the corrected run.

RESULT: yes 216, partial 32, no 1222 (of 1470). Of the 1222 'no', 969 are .jpg/.png screenshots -- a transcript never holds binary image bytes, so these were always going to be 'no' by this method, but they cost nothing but a re-run of whatever capture tool made them; not a real loss. The other 253 'no' files are real content (146 .js, 68 .md, 28 .css, plus a few .json/.jsonl) with zero Read/Write/Edit trace anywhere in the transcript archive (which itself only goes back to 2026-08-27) -- these are the ones actually gone for good as far as this search can tell, on top of the 32 partial (fragment-only) files.

KNOWN LIMITS of the recoverability method, stated plainly rather than hidden in a caveat: (1) it only sees Claude tool calls (Read/Write/Edit) -- a file rewritten via the Bash tool (sed, a heredoc, a script) or by the owner directly in an editor leaves no trace here and reads as 'no' even if it truly changed; reset-recovery's own ask.js finding (a stale pre-edit Read exists, but the file demonstrably changed again afterward with no Write/Edit anywhere on record) is exactly this case, and I kept their 'no' verdict rather than my method's naive 'yes'. (2) A 'yes' verdict means a transcript holds a snapshot as of its last recorded touch -- if a file was edited again by unlogged means after that, the 'yes' content is stale, not final, and this method cannot detect that. Both limits are inherent to reconstructing from transcripts, not fixable within this task's fence.

Did not restore anything, per the brief -- lost.jsonl (1470 lines, replacing the 39-line draft) is the deliverable, and public/framework/ai/2026-09-19/reset-recovery/page.js's top line now states the real total instead of 'roughly a hundred more'. Read-only over the repo throughout except reset-scope/** and the two named reset-recovery files; no git command beyond status/log/diff/reflog/ls-files was run.

Scratch work (the mtime dump, the transcript index, the classifier and its output) lives only in this session's scratchpad, not the repo -- reproducible from the method described above, not needed for the deliverable itself.

assign.outcome: **The reset destroyed 1,470 files' worth of uncommitted work, not ~39 -- 216 are fully recoverable, 285 are gone for good, the rest are replaceable screenshots.** Found the true scope mechanically: every tracked file whose mtime exactly matches the reset's own timestamp (1,043 -- matches the mastermind's own independent count exactly) plus 422 brand-new files that were `git add`-staged but never committed, which a hard reset deletes outright. Built a one-time index of every Read/Write/Edit in the transcript archive and graded all 1,470: 216 `yes` (a full file capture exists and is cited), 32 `partial` (only a diff fragment), 1,222 `no` (969 of those are regenerated screenshots -- cheap to redo -- leaving 253 real files with zero trace, plus the 32 partials, as the actual unrecoverable loss). Caught and fixed one mistake in my own method along the way: an early pass trusted evidence from before the last commit, which wrongly called one file recoverable off a stale, already-committed edit. Restored nothing, per the brief -- the graded list is the deliverable.
